newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Record N.Korean defection on China "Freedom Road".
newsitem.headline: Record N.Korean defection on China "Freedom Road".

text.p: Seventeen North Koreans made an undercover journey across the length of China to Hong Kong in the biggest single defection from the Stalinist nation, Seoul officials said on Thursday.

In a month-long trek down what is becoming the most popular "Freedom Road" for people fleeing North Korea, the group went from one safe house to another in China before sneaking into Hong Kong on November 23. Their journey began on October 26.
The group was helped by ethnic Koreans in China who were paid to act as guides by relatives of the escapees in the United States.
All but one of the 17, who included five children and a pregnant woman, were related, Foreign Ministry spokesman Suh Dae-woon told reporters. The other defector was a North Korean security official.
One of the group was the daughter of Choi Young-do, a defector now living in the United States, Suh said.
He said all 17, who were now in a refugee camp in Hong Kong, had asked for asylum in South Korea. They were expected to arrive in Seoul early next week.
Hong Kong authorities, caught in a delicate diplomatic position by the group's arrival, stonewalled inquiries about them and refused all comment.
The previous largest single defection was in 1987 when North Korean doctor Kim Man-chol, his wife and nine other relatives came to the South via Japan.
"China is now the easiest route for North Koreans to flee their country," said Hun Moon-young, a senior researcher at the state-financed Research Institute for National Unification.
"North Korea's border with the South is heavily fortified, sea-borne escape to Japan is not easy, but China is just across a river," he said.
In May, Chung Kab-ryol, a scientist at Pyongyang's state research institute, and Chang Hae-song, a scriptwriter, also escaped to Hong Kong via China, ending up in South Korea.
Chang fled to China after a conversation in which he criticised North Korean leader Kim Jong-il was reported to authorities. Chung broke away from a group he was travelling with in China.

Yu Suk-ryul, a senior fellow at the Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security, said he expected more escapes from North Korea during the winter when the Yalu and Tumen rivers, which separate North Korea from China, are frozen.
"There are probably going be more people risking their lives to flee hunger and poverty," he said.
A total of 34 North Koreans, excluding the present 17, have defected from the Stalinist state to South Korea this year. There were 38 defections last year and 50 in 1994.
Among North Koreans who sought asylum this year were a pilot in his MiG-19 and a diplomat at North Korea's Zambian embassy.
Seoul analysts say the Stalinist administration is breaking down under acute food and energy shortages and economic difficulties.
Red Cross officials have said North Korea faces a long-term problem in feeding itself after floods and heavy rains this year and last year destroyed much of its arable land.
North Korea estimates this year's rice harvest will be two million tonnes short of target, a shortfall of 40 percent of the grain needed to feed its 26 million people through 1997.
